name: argminmax
baseline: scalar Rust argmin+argmax loop (the repo's own scalar_* benchmark rows)
workload: Single-pass argmin and argmax over a long random array (about 100k elements) for i8..u64, f16, f32 and f64, runtime-dispatched SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON kernels versus a scalar loop.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Benchmarks on my laptop (AMD Ryzen 7 4800U, 1.8 GHz, 16GB RAM) using criterion show that the function is 3-20x faster than the scalar implementation (depending of data type)'. benches/results rows, Ryzen 7 4800U: i16 scalar 74.039 us vs impl 4.4617 us (about 16.6x, derived from page data); i8 scalar 76.858 us vs impl 7.2931 us (about 10.5x, derived); f32 scalar 65.058 us vs impl 11.186 us (about 5.8x, derived). i7-1185G7: f32 scalar 55.549 us vs impl 6.9749 us (about 8.0x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly-2026-10-06 pinned in rust-toolchain.toml (toolchain used for older result rows not stated); cargo bench with criterion, no extra RUSTFLAGS stated; benches/bench_*.rs per element type
hardware: Results file lists Intel i7-1185G7 laptop, AMD Ryzen 7 4800U laptop, AMD Ryzen 5 2600X desktop, Xeon E5-2650 v2 server, Raspberry Pi 3B (ARMv7) and Pi 4B (AArch64); README headline uses the Ryzen 7 4800U
stars_or_usage: 64 stars; implements traits for ndarray and Arrow arrays
tradeoffs: x86-64 (SSE, AVX, AVX2, AVX-512) and AArch64 NEON; 32-bit ARM NEON needs nightly; i128 and u128 use the scalar path; NaN handling is ignore-NaN or return-first-NaN variants (ignore-NaN variant is advertised as 5-30% faster); inner loop is branch-free so runtime does not depend on data order.
caveats: Baseline is the library's own scalar loop, not a third-party library such as NumPy or std iterators. Several rows are annotated slower than an earlier version (for example avx_random_long_f32 'slower than in v0.3'). AVX-512 is slower than SSE for some i8 and u8 rows on the i7-1185G7. The toolchain pin is the current HEAD value and may differ from the one used to produce older rows; no RUSTFLAGS are stated.
found_via: GitHub: candidate from a review of Rust SIMD crates (seed query adapted to Rust); README, benches/results and rust-toolchain.toml opened

name: tphakala/simd
baseline: pure-Go scalar loops (same binary with SIMD_DISABLE=all, or each operation's *Go reference function)
workload: Vectorized slice math (arithmetic, reductions, statistics, distances, activation functions, int8/int16/int32 DSP) on 1024-element float64 and float32 slices, SIMD path versus pure Go, on x86-64 AVX+FMA and ARM64 NEON.
claimed_speedup: README Performance Notes: 'Explicit SIMD ranges from roughly 2-6x on memory-bound elementwise operations up to 10-16x on reductions and fused kernels'. float64 on i7-1260P, 1024 elements: DotProduct 54 ns vs 887 ns (16.5x), EuclideanDistance 15.4x, Mean 12.7x, Sum 12.1x, Clamp 10.6x, Add 2.4x, Div 2.0x, CumulativeSum 1.0x. ARM64 NEON: float32 3.5x-5.2x, float64 2.4x-2.6x. Activation functions: 'Tanh: 73x speedup for f32', Exp 19x for f32.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 toolchain (go.mod minimum 1.25); 'task bench' and 'task bench:compare'; performance CPU governor; best of repeated runs; Variance/StdDev rows re-measured as medians of 9 rounds pinned to one P-core
hardware: Intel Core i7-1260P (AVX+FMA) and Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76, NEON)
tradeoffs: Pure Go assembly (Go assembler, no cgo); AVX-512, AVX+FMA, AVX, SSE2, NEON, NEON+FP16 tiers with runtime detection; amd64 minimum tier differs per package; ARM64 and x86-64 only, pure Go fallback elsewhere; approximate transcendental functions.
caveats: Baseline is the library's own pure-Go loop, and the README notes Go 1.26 generates tighter scalar loops than older toolchains, shrinking elementwise gains. The 73x Tanh and 19x Exp figures compare a fast approximation (max relative error about 7e-6 for f32) with the exact math.Tanh and math.Exp. Hardware is two consumer machines; comparisons shown are against the pure-Go path only, not another Go SIMD library.

name: kelindar/simd
baseline: generic pure-Go implementation inside the same package
workload: Element-wise add/sub/mul/div and sum/min/max reductions on uint8..uint64, int and float slices of 256, 4096 and 16384 elements; clang auto-vectorized C translated to Plan9 assembly (AVX2 on amd64, NEON on arm64).
claimed_speedup: README tables on an i7-13700K: uint8 sum 16384 elements 52.57x, uint8 min 4096 55.02x, uint16 min 16384 84.12x, uint32 sum 16384 10.07x, uint32 add 16384 5.06x, uint8 div 4096 1.19x, uint16 div 16384 0.79x (slower). An Apple M3 Pro table is also given.
compiler_and_flags: Go benchmark output shown (goos/goarch/pkg/cpu); Go version not stated in the README; assembly generated from C with clang
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i7-13700K (Windows, amd64) and Apple M3 Pro (darwin, arm64)
tradeoffs: AVX2 on amd64 and NEON on arm64 only; generic Go fallback otherwise; README lists reductions (Sum, Min, Max) and element-wise Add, Sub, Mul, Div; the Div rows show about 1x.
caveats: Several rows exceed 50x (min/max up to 84x) against a generic Go loop, which may mean the generic Go baseline is slow rather than the SIMD path being near its limit; capped at C because the Go version and the baseline code are not stated in the README. Division rows give about 1x or slower.

name: vek
baseline: pure-Go fallback of the same library (plain Go loops)
workload: In-place float32 and float64 vector operations (Add, Mul, Abs, Sum, Round, Sqrt, Pow, Exp, Log, Max, Find, comparisons, boolean And/All) on 1k and 100k element slices, plus MatMul and 4x4 matrix multiply.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Fast, average speedups of 10x for float32 vectors'. Table at 100k elements: vek32.Sum 65,007 ns Go vs 3,191 ns SIMD (20x), vek32.Exp 1,120,300 vs 49,694 ns (22x), vek32.Log 16x, vek32.Add 6x, vek.Add 2x, vek.MatMul 7x and vek32.MatMul 14x at m=n=p=1k, vek.And 139x.
compiler_and_flags: go test -benchmem -timeout 0 -run=^# -bench=. ./internal/... ; Go version not stated
tradeoffs: AVX2 and FMA on x86-64 only (acceleration disabled by default on macOS, no ARM kernels); behavior undefined on NaN or Inf inputs; minor precision differences from math.Exp, Pow and Log.
caveats: CPU model, Go version and run count are not stated, so the table is first-party numbers only. The 139x row is the boolean vek.And operation; Quantile shows 1x. Last commit is a README note on fast math optimizations.

name: md5-simd
workload: Parallel (multi-buffer) MD5 over 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX-512) concurrent streams, 32 KB to 8 MB per hash, aggregate MB/s versus crypto/md5.
claimed_speedup: README: 'up to 4x faster' with AVX2 and 'up to 8x faster' with AVX512. BenchmarkParallel/8MB-4: crypto/md5 2182.48 MB/s vs AVX2 8748.22 MB/s (4.01x) vs AVX-512 17252.88 MB/s (7.91x). Single-thread block function: crypto/md5 687.66 MB/s, Block8 4144.80 MB/s, Block16 8228.88 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Go benchmarks compared with benchcmp; Go version not stated
hardware: AWS EC2 c5.xlarge, Xeon Platinum 8124M @ 3.0 GHz
tradeoffs: Speedup needs many concurrent hashes (a server collects up to 16 lanes); a single hash or one or two inputs use the scalar path and see no speedup; writes should be multiples of 32 KB; AVX2 uses two cores for more than 8 lanes; amd64 only.
caveats: Throughput is aggregate across lanes and cores, not per-hash latency, so it is a multi-buffer win rather than faster MD5 for one message. Benchmark Go version and flags missing. Baseline crypto/md5 is the default Go standard-library MD5.

name: simd-adler32

claimed_speedup: README, i5-8300H Windows 10: 10k simd-adler32 212.61 ns (43.805 GiB/s) vs adler32 4.8084 us (1.9369 GiB/s) vs adler 17.979 us (530.43 MiB/s) vs wuffs 3843 ns (2.63 GiB/s); i9-9880H macOS: 46.480 GiB/s vs adler32 2.2433 GiB/s; Apple M3 Pro: 37.090 GiB/s vs adler32 3.3894 GiB/s vs adler2 6.1280 GiB/s.

hardware: Intel i5-8300H @ 2.30GHz (Windows 10 Pro), MacBookPro16,1 Intel i9-9880H @ 2.30GHz, MacBook Pro 14 Apple M3 Pro

caveats: Ratio against the adler crate is about 85x (derived from page data, 43.805 GiB/s vs 530.43 MiB/s), which exceeds 50x; the wuffs row ran through a different harness (gcc under mingw64). Compiler version and flags are not stated, so capped at C.

name: SimpleSIMD
baseline: naive scalar loop over int[] (Sum), BenchmarkDotNet 'Naive' row
workload: Sum over an int[] of 10 to 100000 elements using System.Numerics.Vector<T> based helpers versus a plain loop, plus a value-delegate versus Func benchmark.
claimed_speedup: README BenchmarkDotNet table: length 10000 SIMD 585.275 ns vs Naive 3,938.198 ns (ratio 0.15, about 6.7x, derived from page data); length 1000 66.018 ns vs 388.244 ns (ratio 0.17); length 100000 7,325.734 ns vs 40,283.073 ns (ratio 0.19); length 10 3.556 ns vs 5.357 ns (0.66).
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.2, .NET SDK 7.0.100, .NET 7.0.0 X64 RyuJIT AVX2, DefaultJob
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U 1.80GHz (4 cores, 8 logical), Windows 11
tradeoffs: Uses portable Vector<T> (width follows the CPU); value delegates (struct generics) are needed to keep lambdas inlined; targets .NET 7 generic math.
caveats: The benchmark source is not visible at the repo root (folders Generator, SimpleSIMD, Tests), so only the README table is checkable, which is why this is C rather than A. Only Sum is benchmarked, against a plain loop rather than LINQ Sum; the LinqFaster README says that as of .NET 9 much of this SIMD work moved into the runtime LINQ.

name: LitMath
baseline: naive scalar loop over System.Math.Exp and System.Math.Log (NaiveExpDouble, NaiveLogDouble); also claims to beat Intel MKL vector exp for arrays under 2000 elements
workload: AVX2 and AVX-512 double-precision Exp, Log and other math functions on arrays of 64 and 100000 doubles.
claimed_speedup: README BenchmarkDotNet table: Exp N=100000 NaiveExpDouble 354,491.80 ns vs LitExpDouble 64,727.96 ns (about 5.5x, derived from page data); Log N=100000 259,985.93 ns vs 35,793.39 ns (about 7.3x, derived); N=64 Exp 218.69 ns vs 42.34 ns, Log 137.06 ns vs 24.89 ns. name: Quickenshtein
baseline: naive baseline Levenshtein implementation in the repo, and Fastenshtein (other fast .NET Levenshtein library)
workload: Levenshtein edit distance of 10, 400 and 8000 character strings in BenchmarkDotNet, with AVX2/SSE4.1 intrinsics, optional threading, on .NET Framework 4.7.2 and .NET Core 5.0.
claimed_speedup: docs/OverallComparison.md, .NET Core 5.0, 8000 characters: Baseline 356,315,300 ns, Quickenshtein 17,253,112.5 ns (20.92x speedup column), Fastenshtein 82,207,344.4 ns (4.39x); Quickenshtein is about 4.8x faster than Fastenshtein (derived from page data). 400 characters: 64,781.7 ns vs Fastenshtein 342,278.1 ns. IntrinsicsPerformance.md: all intrinsics 17.31 ms, without AVX2 28.94 ms, no intrinsics 100.04 ms.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.12.1, .NET Core SDK 5.0.201, .NET Core 5.0.4 and .NET Framework 4.8 (4.7.2 target), ShortRun job IterationCount=3 LaunchCount=1 WarmupCount=3
tradeoffs: Uses hardware intrinsics with scalar fallback; optional multi-threading allocates a little; the benchmark shows large gains only with SSE4.1 and AVX2 enabled (disabling SSE4.1 gives the no-intrinsics time).
caveats: Slower than Fastenshtein on 10-character strings on .NET Core 5.0 (317.7 ns vs 181.4 ns). Only three iterations per ShortRun, so errors are wide. Benchmarks ran on .NET Core 5.0 and .NET Framework 4.8. I did not open the benchmark project source, only the repo's docs and README statement that the benchmarks are in the repository.

name: gohashtree
baseline: minio/sha256-simd (Go SHA-256 with AVX-512 and SHA extensions)
workload: SHA-256 over consecutive pairs of 32-byte chunks (Merkle tree layers) in Go assembly based on Intel's multi-buffer implementation, 1 to 16 pairs and large lists, versus minio/sha256-simd.
claimed_speedup: README benchmarks: Xeon with AVX-512, BenchmarkHash_16_minio 7933 ns vs BenchmarkHash_16 1988 ns (about 4.0x, derived from page data), HashLargeList_minio 105,404,666 ns vs HashList 25,368,532 ns (about 4.2x, derived); ARM64 with crypto extensions (darwin): Hash_16 1974 ns vs 689.2 ns (about 2.9x, derived); Raspberry Pi arm64 without crypto extensions: Hash_16 67142 ns vs 13351 ns (about 5.0x, derived). Hash_1 on the Xeon: 473.1 ns vs 391.3 ns.
compiler_and_flags: go test . -bench=. ; Go version not stated
hardware: 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.80GHz' with AVX-512 (model not given), Apple arm64 laptop with crypto extensions (model not given), Raspberry Pi arm64 without crypto extensions

name: numpy-minmax
workload: Minimum and maximum of float32 (and contiguous int16) NumPy arrays in one pass using AVX/AVX512 (README: written in C).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Roughly 2.3x speedup compared to the numpy amin+amax equivalent (tested on Intel CPU with numpy 1.24-1.26)'.
tradeoffs: Fast path for float32 C-contiguous, F-contiguous or 1D strided arrays and contiguous int16; strided arrays with ndim >= 2 fall back to numpy amin/amax with no gain; Linux (arm and x86-64), macOS arm, Windows x86-64 wheels.
caveats: One headline ratio with no table, no CPU model, no compiler or flags; README points to scripts/perf_benchmark.py (which also needs diplib) but the script was not opened. README states it was tested only with numpy 1.24-1.26.

name: java-fast/quad-search
workload: Quaternary narrowing plus a Vector API (jdk.incubator.vector) 16-element block scan versus Arrays.binarySearch over sorted int arrays of 4k to 1m elements, cold-cache and warm-cache JMH runs on Oracle JDK and GraalVM.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperform Arrays.binarySearch by up to 25% on Oracle JDK, up to 16% on GraalVM on Apple M4 ARM64 (Neon 128-bit)' and 'up to 24% on Oracle JDK, up to 29% on GraalVM on x86-64 AMD (AVX2 256-bit)'; p99 better in almost all cases. docs/results/amd64 Oracle JDK 1m cold: binarySearchDefault 1192.757 ns/op, quadSearch 1020.096 ns/op, simdQuadSearch 1053.785 ns/op (about 12% less time for the SIMD variant, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Java 25 (Oracle JDK and GraalVM), JMH sample mode via Gradle (./gradlew jmh); run-benchmarks.sh in repo
hardware: Apple M4 (arm64 NEON) and an AMD x86-64 machine with AVX2 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector (incubator module); int arrays only; same return semantics as Arrays.binarySearch.
caveats: Gains are modest (about 10 to 29%). In the 1m cold sample file the non-SIMD quadSearch variant beat the SIMD variant, so the win comes mostly from quaternary narrowing and cache behaviour rather than SIMD. Idea credited to a Daniel Lemire blog post. CPU models are not stated, so tier C although JMH files are in the repo.
